name: Antichrist
title: The lawless one, the deceiver and God's adversary
summary: Antichrist is a central figure in New Testament and Christian eschatology, known as the ultimate opponent of Christ and his people. The term 'antichrist' appears exclusively in the letters of John, where the apostle uses it both for any spirit or person who denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, and as a prophetic pointer toward an end-time figure who will deceive many. Paul refers to a related figure as "the lawless one" and "the son of destruction" – one who will exalt himself above everything called God and even set himself up in God's temple. In Revelation this opponent is linked to "the beast from the sea", which is given power over the peoples of the earth and wages war against the saints, but which is finally completely defeated at Christ's return. Old Testament prophecies, especially in Daniel concerning "the little horn" and the arrogant king, form an important background for these New Testament ideas. In this way several biblical traditions are woven together into the picture of a final opponent who ultimately bows under God's sovereign power.

keyEvents.title: Old Testament background in Daniel
keyEvents.description: Daniel's prophecies about a little horn that speaks great words against the Most High, and a king who exalts himself above every god, form an important background for New Testament concepts of the Antichrist.

keyEvents.title: The warning about many antichrists
keyEvents.description: The apostle John warns the churches that many antichrists have already appeared, who deny the Father and the Son. This is a sign that the last hour has come.

keyEvents.title: Testing the Spirits
keyEvents.description: John urges believers to test the spirits, for many false prophets have gone out into the world. Every spirit that does not confess Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is the spirit of the antichrist.

keyEvents.title: The Deceiver's Mark
keyEvents.description: In his second letter, John identifies the deceiver and the antichrist as the one who does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

keyEvents.title: The Lawless One Revealed
keyEvents.description: Paul describes the lawless one who will appear before the day of the Lord. He will set himself up in God's temple, claiming to be God, but the Lord Jesus will destroy him with the breath of his mouth.

keyEvents.title: The Beast from the Sea in Revelation
keyEvents.description: John sees in a vision a beast rising out of the sea, which is given authority over every tribe and nation. It makes war against the saints and speaks blasphemies against God, an image traditionally linked to the figure of the antichrist.

keyEvents.title: The Final Defeat of the Beast
keyEvents.description: The beast and the false prophet are ultimately defeated and thrown alive into the lake of fire when Christ returns in glory, marking God's final victory over evil.

versions.title: The Lawless One and God's Adversary
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'leader' is very general and provides little information. The Antichrist should be described with more precise roles that reflect his biblical characteristics: deceiver, opponent of Christ, false ruler, etc.; [minor] The era is set to 'early-church' because the term is first used in the New Testament letters. This is acceptable, but it should be noted that the figure of the Antichrist has an eschatological/end-time character and does not belong exclusively to the time of the early church. Nevertheless, there is no 'eschatological' era in the schema, and 'early-church' is the most suitable option.; [minor] The title is good but could include 'deceiver' to reflect the central role deception plays in the description of the Antichrist, especially in John's writings.; [major] Footnotes are missing. A profile on the Antichrist should have footnotes about the etymology of the term (Greek: antichristos), the historical development of the concept of the Antichrist, and the relationship between the various New Testament traditions (Johannine vs. Pauline vs. apocalyptic).; [minor] One might consider including Daniel's prophecies about a future ruler (Dan 7:25, Dan 9:27, Dan 11:36-39) as Old Testament background for the figure of the Antichrist, since these texts are traditionally linked to the same prophetic tradition.

versions.reason: [minor] The Antichrist is primarily an eschatological figure who does not belong to one specific time period. 'early-church' is defensible because the concept was first formulated in the early church (the Johannine letters, Paul), but one could also argue that this is a cross-cutting figure. Nevertheless, 'early-church' is the best available option.; [minor] The summary is well written and theologically balanced. A small improvement can be made by clarifying that the term 'Antichrist' as an independent designation occurs only in the Johannine letters, while the other New Testament texts use other designations for the same or related figures.; [minor] In the event 'The final defeat of the beast', it may be useful to also include Revelation 20:10 where the devil himself is cast into the lake of fire, to complete the picture of the final confrontation. This is optional since the focus here is on the beast/Antichrist.

footnotes.text: The Greek word 'antichristos' (ἀντίχριστος) appears only in the letters of John (1 John 2:18, 2:22, 4:3; 2 John 1:7). The prefix 'anti-' can mean both 'against' and 'in place of', reflecting that the antichrist is both an opponent of Christ and one who seeks to replace him.

In early Christian tradition, the figure of the antichrist was often identified with specific historical persons. Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 180 AD) linked the number of the beast, 666, to various names, while several Church Fathers pointed to the Roman emperor Nero as an early fulfillment of the prophecy. The Nero redivivus myth—the belief that Nero would return—may have influenced Revelation's imagery of the beast whose fatal wound was healed.

Paul's description of 'the lawless one' (ho anomos) in 2 Thessalonians 2 and John's use of 'antichrist' represent two different but related traditions. Paul emphasizes a single end-time figure who exalts himself in God's temple, while John uses the term both for a future figure and for contemporary false teachers already at work. These traditions were gradually harmonized in later Christian theology.

The book of Daniel, especially chapters 7–12, forms an important Old Testament background for New Testament concepts of the antichrist. The 'little horn' in Daniel 7:8,25 that speaks great words against the Most High, and the king in Daniel 11:36 who exalts himself above every god, were interpreted in Jewish and early Christian tradition as prototypes of the final opponent of God.

In rabbinic tradition there is no direct parallel to the Christian figure of the antichrist, but the concept of Armilus—a villainous end-time figure who opposes the Messiah—developed in later Jewish apocalyptic literature and may reflect mutual influence between Jewish and Christian eschatological thought.

The number 666 (or in some manuscripts 616) in Revelation 13:18 has been the subject of intense speculation throughout history. The most widely accepted scholarly interpretation is that it is a gematria-based wordplay, where the Hebrew letters in 'Neron Kaisar' (נרון קסר) yield the numerical value 666, while the Latin form 'Nero Caesar' yields 616—possibly explaining the variants found in the manuscript tradition.
